There were moments of beauty that felt undeserved.
Singing together at dawn.
Sharing bread without knowing where the next meal would come from.
Seeing joy appear on faces hardened by suffering.
In those moments, I felt close to God in a way that required no explanation.
There were also moments of doubt that returned without warning.
I worried that we were too extreme, that our poverty would be misread as condemnation of others.
I worried that people admired us instead of God.
I worried that my own words might be mistaken for wisdom rather than stumbling attempts at faithfulness.
I began to withdraw more often into prayer, seeking silence as a refuge rather than an absence.
In that silence, I sensed that God was asking more of me, though I did not yet know what.
The sweetness that had followed my early obedience was giving way to something heavier, more demanding.
Love, I was learning, matures into endurance.
By the time I realized that my life no longer belonged to me alone, it was too late to turn back.
The brothers looked to me not for perfection, but for direction.
The Church watched us carefully.
The poor expected consistency.
Even creation itself seemed to respond, as if the world had grown attentive to this strange way of living.
I had wanted to become nothing.
Instead, I had been given a place ...
Fragile and dangerous, between obedience and influence ...
Between joy and responsibility.
I did not yet know how costly that place would become.
But I sensed, dimly, that the hardest part of my journey was still ahead.
As the years passed, my body began to betray me long before my heart did.
The roads that once felt light beneath my feet now pressed themselves into my bones.
Hunger, which had once sharpened my prayer, now weakened my strength.
I accepted this reluctantly.
I had believed that love would make me invincible.
Instead, it taught me how fragile a man can be when he gives himself without reserve.
People began to speak of me in ways that made me uneasy.
They called me holy.
They repeated my words as if they carried weight beyond their intention.
I wanted to interrupt them, to insist that I was still learning, still stumbling.
But admiration is difficult to silence once it takes root.
I retreated more often, seeking solitude not because I despised people, but because I feared forgetting who I truly was before God.
It was during these years that creation itself became my companion.
Not as metaphor, not as poetry, but as family.
I spoke to the birds because I believed they belonged to the same hand that had shaped me.
I called the sun my brother and the moon my sister because I had learned that possession was a lie.
Nothing belonged to me, and I belonged to everything God had made.
When people laughed at this, I did not correct them.
Love does not require explanation.
Yet love, when lived honestly, demands more than affection.
It demands reconciliation.
When I encountered the wolf that terrorized the town, I did not see a beast to be conquered.
I saw fear meeting fear.
I spoke to it not as a master, but as a brother out of place.
When peace followed, others called it a miracle.
I called it obedience.
Violence ends where listening begins.
Even joy, however, could not shield me from the weight of leadership.
The brothers had grown numerous.
Some desired stricter rules.
Others desired comfort.
I stood between them ...
Aching with the knowledge that I could not satisfy every longing without betraying the simplicity we had been given.
There were nights when I wept alone, asking God why love so often feels like division.
During this time, Clare came into her vocation.
Her courage humbled me.
She chose poverty with a clarity that reminded me of my own beginning, and I struggled to step aside and let her path unfold without interference.
I had learned to renounce possessions; I was still learning to renounce control.
Trust, I discovered, is obedience extended to others.
My health worsened.
My sight dimmed.
Pain settled into my body like an unwelcome guest who refused to leave.
I fasted beyond wisdom, believing suffering itself might clarify God's will.
Instead, it deepened my dependence.
I was forced to accept care, something I had resisted fiercely.
To be fed, to be guided, to be restrained from my own excesses
This humbled me more than public nakedness ever had.
It was in this weakened state that I withdrew into prayer, seeking only quiet, asking for nothing.
I had ceased to desire signs.
I wanted only fidelity.
It was then that the suffering of Christ pressed itself upon me in a way I had never imagined or sought.
The wounds came not as glory, but as terror.
Pain seared through me, sudden and overwhelming.
I hid them as best I could, ashamed not of the suffering, but of the attention it might draw.
I had not asked for this.
I did not feel worthy of it.
If it meant anything, it meant union, and union is costly.
From that day forward, my body became both prayer and burden.
Each movement reminded me of the distance between who I was and who I was called to be.
Yet even in this, there was mercy.
Suffering stripped away what little remained of my desire to be understood.
It left only trust.
As my sight faded, I learned to see differently.
Sounds sharpened.
Touch carried meaning.
I listened more.
I spoke less.
When bitterness threatened, I resisted it with praise, not because I felt it, but because I chose it.
Gratitude, I learned, is an act of defiance against despair.
It was during this darkness that I composed my final song.
I praised God for the sun, for the moon, for fire and water, for those who forgive, for those who endure.
I even praised Him for death, though the words trembled as I spoke them.
If death was to come, I wanted to meet it as a brother, not an enemy.
I asked forgiveness of those I had wronged, knowingly or not.
I reconciled with my father in my heart long before I could do so in words.
I released the brothers from the burden of imitating me perfectly.
I told them to follow Christ, not Francis.
I had always feared being remembered for myself rather than for the love I tried to live.
When the end approached, I felt no certainty, only peace.
Faith does not erase doubt; it teaches you how to carry it without fear.
I had not become holy by escaping the world, but by belonging to it fully, without claiming ownership.
I was not born poor.
I became poor.
I was not born obedient.
I learned obedience through failure.
I was not born a saint.
I was formed slowly, painfully, through mercy.
If my life has any meaning, let it be this: that nothing is wasted when offered freely, and that love ...
When given without reserve, will always lead you farther than you intended to go.
That is not a warning.
It is an invitation.
St. Jude Thaddaeus
What Was Thought Lost
Dear friend, I am Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James.
Even as I say it, I feel the old ache of having to explain.
Not Judas.
Not the one who betrayed the Lord.
That name
So common among our people
Became a wound the night the kiss was given in the garden.
After that, whenever someone heard “Judas,” their faces tightened as if the word itself carried a blade.
So I learned to add another name, as if I could shelter my soul behind it: Thaddeus.
Some called me Lebbaeus.
I did not mind what they called me, so long as they did not confuse me with the dead man whose memory still tasted of iron.
I was not the loudest among the Twelve.
I was not the first to leave my nets, like Simon and Andrew.
I was not the one who leaned close enough at supper to hear the Lord's breathing, like John.
I was not the one whose doubt became famous, like Thomas.
I was not the one whose keys became a promise to the whole Church, like Peter.
In our days together I was often simply there
Another pair of feet on the dusty road, another set of hands passing bread, another voice murmuring the psalms at dawn.
And yet I was called.
I remember the day more by its weight than by its details.
The air had that bright, dry sharpness you find near midday, when the shadows huddle tight beneath stones.
We had been following Him already
Some of us from curiosity, some from hunger ...
Some from desperation, some because His words burned in us like a coal we could not spit out.
He had spent the night in prayer.
When He came down, there was a stillness around Him, as if the world itself waited for His next step.
He chose us one by one.
He did not choose us the way men choose soldiers, measuring muscle and steadiness.
He chose as if He saw a hidden seam inside each of us, and with a single look He could split open what was false and call forth what was true.
When His eyes met mine, I felt exposed and known
Worse than that, I felt invited.
Not to comfort, but to a life that would not belong to me anymore.
There is a kind of mercy in being overlooked, you know.
In a crowded room, the one who is not noticed can listen.
He can see who reaches for the best seat, who pretends not to ...
Who avoids another's gaze, who laughs too loudly to hide a fear.
I listened a great deal in those days.
I listened to the Lord speak of the Kingdom as if it were both coming and already here.
I listened to Him speak of the Father with an intimacy that made the learned men bristle and the simple ones weep.
I listened to Him speak of mercy like a man offering water to the thirsty, and of judgment like a man warning of a fire that cannot be charmed away.
And I listened to what people whispered about Him.
Some said He was Elijah.
Some said John the Baptizer, raised up again.
Some said a prophet.
Some said a blasphemer.
Some said the Son of David.
I heard my own heart say words I did not yet have courage to shape: Could He be the One?
If you want to know what it was like to walk with Him, imagine living beside a river that never runs dry.
Every day, people came to Him with their jars
Some cracked, some clean, some stolen, some empty for the first time in years.
And He filled them.
Not always the way they wanted.
Not always with what they asked for.
But always with what was true.
I saw Him touch a leper, and the man did not pull away from the touch, because no one had touched him in so long he had forgotten what warmth felt like.
I saw a woman weeping behind Him, pressing her tears into His feet like an offering, and I saw Him receive it as naturally as He received bread.
I saw Him speak to the wind as if it were a creature that understood obedience, and it did.
There were times I thought I understood Him, and then He would speak and I would realize I had built a little house of expectations around His words, and He had never agreed to live in it.
We argued among ourselves like brothers do.
We were ashamed of it, later, but it is the truth.
We argued about who was greatest.
We argued about the right way to speak to strangers, about whether children should be kept back ...
About whether to call down fire on those who refused Him.
We thought we were defending Him when we were really defending our own pride.
He was patient with us, not as a man indulging fools, but as a teacher who knows that clay must be worked again and again before it holds water.
Sometimes I watched Him and wondered where His patience came from.
His eyes
People speak of miracles as if they were tricks, but I tell you, His gaze was its own miracle.
He could look at a man sunk in sin and see not only the sin, but the man beneath it.
He could look at a hypocrite and name the hypocrisy without forgetting that even hypocrites are loved.
Once, near the end
Though we did not know it was near the end
He spoke words that lodged in me like a thorn.
He said that the world would hate us.
I had lived under Rome.
I knew what hatred looked like when it wore armor.
I knew what it looked like when it wore a priestly robe.
But I did not know what it would mean for the world to hate men who carried no sword, only a message.
We were in the upper room, the air thick with oil and sweat and the scent of roasted lamb.
The lamps shook slightly as if they, too, were nervous.
He spoke of going away.
He spoke of preparing a place.
He spoke of giving us peace, though not as the world gives peace.
All of it felt like standing on the edge of a cliff in the dark, hearing the sea below.
And there, in the middle of that holy sorrow, a question rose in me that I could not keep down.
I asked it not to challenge Him but because the confusion in my chest demanded words.
“Lord, ” I said ...

“How is it that You will manifest Yourself to us, and not to the world?”
Even as I asked it ...
I heard my own expectation.
I expected a revelation like lightning
Something that would force every knee down at once.
I expected the Messiah to sweep the earth like a storm, leaving no doubt behind.
If He was who He claimed to be, why would He not show Himself in a way the world could not deny?
Why would the Holy One move quietly, as if He were a secret?
He looked at me
Not irritated, not dismissive, but steady.
And He answered in a way that did not feed my desire for spectacle.
He spoke of love.
He said that whoever loves Him will keep His word, and the Father will love him, and They will come to him and make Their dwelling with him.
Do you hear how strange that is?
Not “I will build you a throne.” Not “I will topple Rome.” Not “I will make the world applaud you.” But: We will come to you.
We will dwell with you.
He spoke of God not as a distant judge but as a Guest who enters the house of a faithful heart.
It was not the answer my impatient mind wanted.
It was deeper than that.
It suggested that the Kingdom would not begin with conquest, but with communion.
That the Lord would win the world not by crushing it, but by entering it
One life at a time
Through love.
I did not grasp it fully then.
I only felt its weight.
In the days that followed, I began to notice a pattern.
When He performed signs, He often told people not to speak of them.
When crowds grew wild with excitement, He withdrew.
When they wanted to make Him king, He slipped away like a man avoiding praise.
It was as if He refused to be handled by the world's hunger for power.
He would not let Himself be used as proof for the pride of men.
And then came the night when everything broke.
The garden was cold.
The air had that damp heaviness that clings to your skin.
We tried to stay awake, but grief is a kind of sleep, and it kept pulling us down.
He went to pray, and we heard Him a little way off ...
Pouring Himself out to the Father with a pain that made the hair on my arms rise.
I wanted to be brave.
I wanted to stay near Him.
But my body betrayed me.
I slept when I should have watched.
When the torches came, it looked like the world had caught fire.
Shadows leapt on the olive trunks.
Soldiers' boots trampled the grass.
And then that kiss
Soft as a lover's greeting, sharp as a dagger.
Judas.
The name became poison in my mouth.
After that, we scattered.
I will not dress it up for you: I ran.
The others ran, too, or hid, or followed at a distance with their hearts in their throats.
There is a shame in remembering your own fear, but there is also truth.
If you are seeking saints made of stone, you will be disappointed.
The Lord did not choose statues; He chose men.
I remember the courtyard where Peter stood near the fire, and I remember the sound of a rooster in the dark, and I remember the way Peter's face collapsed when the truth of his denial reached him.
I remember thinking, then, that we were all capable of betrayal
Not always with a kiss, but with cowardice.
When they crucified Him, the sky itself seemed to grieve.
The day turned wrong.
The air tasted of dust and blood.
I stood far enough away to keep from being recognized, close enough that the cries reached my bones.
I had seen death before; anyone who has lived under Rome has seen it.
But this was not simply death.
It was the death of the Innocent.
It was the death of the One who had spoken as no man ever spoke.
And the worst of it was the silence inside me.
Not silence as peace
Silence as absence.
Like a room whose hearth has gone cold.
All the questions returned, sharp and cruel.
If He was the Messiah, how could He be nailed like a criminal?
If He was the Holy One, how could He be mocked?
If He was the Son, where was the Father?
In those hours I understood something about my own question in the upper room.
I had asked why He would reveal Himself to us and not to the world.
Now I saw the world staring right at Him and still not seeing.
The soldiers saw a condemned man.
The passersby saw entertainment.
The leaders saw a threat removed.
Even some of His followers saw only catastrophe.
To see Him as He truly was required more than eyes.
It required a heart willing to be changed.
When they took His body down, I felt as if the ground beneath the whole world had shifted.
We gathered behind locked doors like frightened children.
We spoke in whispers.
Every footstep outside made us flinch.
We did not yet understand that the Kingdom we thought would come with banners was about to come like a seed splitting open underground.
I thought of His words: that the Father and He would make Their dwelling with those who love Him.
I wondered how love could survive this.
I wondered how a dwelling could be made in a heart that felt gutted.
And yet, even there
Behind those locked doors
Something remained.
Not certainty.
Not strength.
But a small stubborn ember: the memory of His gaze, the weight of His words ...
The taste of His peace that did not depend on circumstances.
We were at the edge of Act I without knowing it
At the point where a story either ends in despair or turns toward a mystery too large to name.
We thought we had lost everything.
But the Lord had told us He would come to us.
And if He spoke truth
As He always did
Then even our fear, even our confusion, even our shame, would become the place where God chose to dwell.
After His burial, time lost its shape.
Day and night no longer felt like opposites, only like different shades of waiting.
We measured hours by fear: the scrape of sandals outside, the knock that never came ...
The rumors that drifted through the city like smoke.
Jerusalem had always been loud, but now every sound felt sharpened, as if the world itself had turned hostile.
We prayed, but our prayers stumbled.
We remembered His words, but they clashed against the sight of the cross.
We told ourselves the psalms had room for sorrow, that the prophets had spoken of suffering ...
That the righteous man is often crushed.
Still, it felt like trying to hold water in our hands.
And then
He came.
I struggle to find language that does not cheapen that moment.
If I say “He appeared,” it sounds like a trick.
If I say “He entered,” it sounds ordinary.
But the truth is this: He stood among us as if death had been a door He simply chose not to keep shut.
The wounds were there.
We saw them.
He did not erase them.
He did not pretend the cross had not happened.
He carried it with Him into the room, transformed but unmistakable.
“Peace be with you,” He said.
Not accusation.
Not rebuke.
Peace.
I felt something inside me give way, not like a wall collapsing, but like a knot loosening that I had not known was strangling me.
Fear did not vanish all at once, but it lost its authority.
Death no longer felt final.
Failure no longer felt definitive.
Everything He had said
Every strange, impossible promise
Suddenly stood upright and solid.
In those days after His rising, we learned how small our understanding had been.
He opened the Scriptures to us, not as a scholar showing off his knowledge, but as a friend revealing the hidden structure of a familiar house.
Moses, the prophets, the psalms
All of it converged in Him.
Suffering was not an interruption.
It was the path.
Still, even then, confusion clung to us.
We asked if the kingdom would be restored now.
We wanted timetables, clarity, resolution.
He gave us something else.
He gave us a commission.
We were to go out, not with swords, not with force, but with witness.
We were to speak of repentance and forgiveness, of mercy offered to sinners, of life stronger than death.
We were to go to the ends of the earth with a message the earth did not yet know how to receive.
When He ascended, my heart ached again
But differently.
This time, the ache was not abandonment.
It was longing.
He did not disappear into absence; He went ahead of us ...
Like a leader who climbs the hill first so that the path might be known.
Then came the Spirit.
I had heard the prophets speak of God pouring out His Spirit, of hearts of stone becoming flesh.
I had never imagined the sound of it
The rush like a violent wind, the crackle of fire that did not burn but illuminated.
It was not frenzy.
It was clarity.
Courage poured into us where fear had lived.
Words rose to our lips that did not belong to any one nation.
The world gathered, and somehow, impossibly, heard itself addressed by God.
From that day, everything accelerated.
The city that had crucified our Lord became the first place where His name was proclaimed openly.
Healings followed
Not as spectacles, but as signs pointing beyond themselves.
The poor heard hope.
The guilty heard forgiveness.
The proud heard a challenge they could not ignore.
And opposition followed just as quickly.
It came first as confusion, then irritation, then anger.
The leaders who had silenced Jesus did not appreciate His voice echoing through us.
They threatened.
They imprisoned.
They beat.
They warned us to stop speaking His name.
We did not stop.
At first, it felt like triumph
That strange exhilaration that comes when obedience seems to be rewarded immediately.
The community grew.
Bread was shared.
Prayer filled our days.
We believed, perhaps foolishly, that the world would see and be convinced.
But faith does not spread in a straight line.
Cracks began to appear
Not only from outside, but within.
Some lied for honor.
Some murmured for fairness.
Some twisted the message, bending grace into permission, freedom into indulgence.
Others demanded signs, always signs, as if trust were a currency they refused to spend.
This was when the weight of my calling pressed hardest on me.
I had never wanted to lead.
I had never wanted a voice that carried authority.
Yet there I was, entrusted with souls ...
With truth, with the fragile early Church that seemed capable of breaking apart under its own growth.
False teachers crept in quietly.
They spoke smooth words.
They promised freedom without repentance, knowledge without obedience, grace without cost.
They appealed to pride, to secret insight, to the ancient temptation to be like gods on our own terms.
I watched confusion spread like a slow infection.
Some began to doubt everything.
Others clung to extremes, harsh where the Lord had been merciful, permissive where He had called for holiness.
The joy we had known did not vanish, but it became strained, like a string pulled too tight.
It was then that I wrote.
Not as a man polishing his thoughts, but as one sounding an alarm.
I wrote because silence would have been a betrayal.
I wrote because faith, left unattended, can erode from within.
I wrote because mercy does not mean pretending that darkness is light.
My words were sharp.
I knew they would be.
They were not meant to flatter.
They were meant to wake the sleeping and steady the trembling.
I warned against those who had slipped in unnoticed, who distorted grace ...
Who denied in practice what they claimed with their lips.
But I also wrote of mercy.
This mattered to me deeply.
It was easy to grow hard in those days, to see danger everywhere and mistake severity for holiness.
Yet I remembered His eyes.
I remembered how He treated doubters, how He did not break the bruised reed or extinguish the smoldering wick.
So I urged them to contend for the faith
And to do so without hatred.
To save some by snatching them from the fire, yes, but to show mercy with fear, aware of their own vulnerability.
To pray in the Spirit.
To remain in the love of God.
To wait for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life.
Those words were not abstract to me.
They were born of nights spent wrestling with despair ...
Of days spent watching faith flicker in others and wondering how long mine would hold.
When I finished the letter, I did not feel relief.
I felt exposed.
Writing truth has a way of doing that
It binds you to the very standard you proclaim.
After that, I traveled.
Where exactly I went, history has blurred.
Roads merge in memory.
Cities blend.
But I remember the faces: suspicious, weary, hungry.
I remember speaking in marketplaces, in homes, in half-ruined synagogues where the air still smelled of old incense.
I remember nights when my words seemed to fall like seed on stone, and mornings when a single conversation bore fruit that astonished me.
I also remember rejection.
Some laughed.
Some argued endlessly.
Some listened politely and then turned away, unwilling to surrender what the message demanded.
Others reacted with fury.
More than once I felt the unmistakable shift in a crowd when curiosity curdles into threat.
The world did not hate us all at once.
It learned to hate us.
And still, I kept going.
Not because I felt brave.
Often I did not.
Not because I was certain of success.
I rarely was.
I kept going because I had seen the Risen Lord.
Because death no longer had the last word.
Because love, once revealed, cannot be un-known.
There were nights I wondered whether any of it mattered.
Whether my name would vanish entirely, whether my labor would be swallowed by stronger voices ...
Whether my faithfulness would dissolve into obscurity.
And in those moments, I remembered my question in the upper room.
Why would He reveal Himself to us and not to the world?
I began, slowly, painfully, to understand the answer.
The revelation was not withheld.
It was entrusted.
Not forced upon the world, but offered through lives willing to be broken open and poured out.
Through witnesses whose strength was not dominance but endurance.
Through men like me
Quiet, uncertain, easily forgotten
Who nevertheless carried a treasure that did not belong to us.
By the time death drew near, I was no longer surprised by it.
I had learned that the Kingdom advances most often through losses that look like failures.
That seeds must fall into the earth and die.
That faith, to be real, must pass through fire.
I did not know how my story would end.
I only knew whom I belonged to.
And that, I discovered, was enough.
Death did not arrive with clarity.
It came the way most endings do
Without ceremony, without an audience that understood what it was witnessing.
I had long since stopped expecting recognition.
The roads I walked had taught me that faithfulness rarely announces itself.
If my life had been a seed, then death was simply the moment it vanished into the earth.
I will not trouble you with the manner of my martyrdom.
Others have argued over tools and methods, over which empire's cruelty finally closed my eyes.
What matters is simpler: I gave what remained of my life to the same Lord who had given His first.
I did not feel heroic.
I felt finished.
Like a sentence reaching its final word.
And then
Silence.
Not the silence of fear, nor the silence of grief, but a vast, gentle stillness.
Time loosened its grip.
The noise of the world faded like a receding shore.
I became aware, not all at once but gradually, that death was not an abyss but a crossing.
That the One who had promised to dwell with those who loved Him had kept His word even here.
I stood, if standing is the right word, in the presence of God.
There are no metaphors that do Him justice.
Every image collapses under the weight of His reality.
Light without glare.
Authority without threat.
Love without limit.
To be seen by Him was to be known completely
And to discover that being known did not mean being rejected.
In that presence, I understood my life differently.
I saw how often I had measured fruit by noise.
How I had expected impact to resemble visibility.
How I had secretly hoped that obedience would earn me a place in memory.
Those expectations fell away like dust.
What remained was truth: that fidelity itself had been the point.
That walking where I was sent, saying what I was given to say, loving whom I was commanded to love
This had been enough.
Centuries passed like breaths.
The world I had known dissolved into history.
Empires shifted.
Languages fractured and reformed.
The Church endured
Wounded, radiant, imperfect, alive.
My name faded.
Even among the faithful, I became a footnote, a shadow behind better-known stories.
I watched this without bitterness.
Obscurity no longer frightened me.
It had become familiar ground.
Then something unexpected happened.
I began to hear my name again.
Not spoken with confidence, but with hesitation.
Not from pulpits, but from kitchens and hospital rooms.
From the mouths of those who had reached the end of their plans and found nothing left to hold.
They spoke my name carefully, as if unsure it would answer.
They spoke it when diagnoses came back wrong.
When debts stacked too high.
When relationships collapsed.
When faith itself felt like a thread worn thin by too many nights of unanswered prayer.
They spoke my name because no one else was listening.
At first, I did not understand why it was happening.
I had not been a miracle worker in life.
I had not been a pillar, a reformer, a founder.
I had been a witness
Quiet, persistent, often uncertain.
Why would desperation find its way to me?
Then I saw the shape of it.
The world had learned my story without reading it.
They sensed, without knowing how, that I belonged to the forgotten corners.
That I knew what it meant to stand near greatness and still feel small.
That I knew how it felt to labor without applause, to believe without reassurance, to hope when evidence had run dry.
They prayed to me because I had lived what they were living.
They prayed because my life whispered something their own hearts needed to hear: that God does not abandon what the world has written off.
Grace moved where they prayed.
Not always as rescue.
Not always as reversal.
But as presence.
As endurance.
As the strange, quiet strength to take the next step when no map remained.
I watched as my name became attached to what people called “lost causes.” The phrase made me smile
Not with irony, but with recognition.
I had been there.
I had stood inside causes that looked lost: a crucified Messiah, a frightened band of disciples ...
A fragile Church riddled with division and danger.
None of them were lost.
They had simply not finished becoming what God intended.
I saw a mother pray through tears, asking not for certainty but for enough peace to sleep.
I saw a man kneel in a church he barely believed in anymore, whispering my name like a last experiment.
I saw prayers scribbled on scraps of paper, tucked into pockets, folded into hands that trembled with fear.
And I understood, finally, the long arc of my life.
The Lord had not chosen me to be remembered quickly.
He had chosen me to be needed later.
My obscurity had not been a flaw.
It had been preparation.
I had learned how to listen because no one was watching.
I had learned how to persist because no one was praising.
I had learned how to trust because outcomes were hidden from me.
Those lessons were not wasted.
They became a bridge between heaven and the places on earth where hope runs thin.
If you are listening to me now, perhaps it is because you recognize something of yourself in my story.
Perhaps you have stood beside others who seemed more gifted, more certain, more visible.
Perhaps you have wondered whether your quiet faith matters in a world that rewards noise.
Perhaps you have prayed and felt the weight of waiting stretch longer than you thought you could endure.
I tell you this not as a patron, but as a brother: God does not despise hidden lives.
He does not measure love by recognition.
He does not abandon work simply because it unfolds slowly.
The Kingdom grows the way my life unfolded
Beneath the surface, through trust, through endurance, through seeds that disappear before they rise.
I once asked the Lord why He would reveal Himself to some and not to the world.
Now I know.
He reveals Himself wherever love makes room for Him.
Sometimes that room is grand and visible.
Often it is small, unnoticed, and trembling.
But He dwells there all the same.
And nothing entrusted to Him
No prayer, no life, no cause the world has given up on
Is ever truly lost.
St. Thérèse of Lisieux
Story of a Soul
It is to you, dear friend, that I confide the story of my soul
Not because it contains anything extraordinary
But because the Good God has loved me in my littleness, and has wished to make known the ways of His mercy through one who is very small.
When I was first asked to write these memories, I feared that looking back might trouble the peace He has given me.
I feared too that I might speak too much of myself.
But obedience has taught me that when God asks, He also gives the grace to respond, and that the simplest way of pleasing Him is to do His will without reasoning.
Before beginning, I knelt before the statue of Our Lady who had so often watched over my childhood.
I begged her to guide my hand ...
That nothing might be written here except what would glorify God and serve the good of souls.
I do not wish to recount my life as one might tell a story; I wish only to sing the mercies of the Lord, for everything that is good in me comes from Him.
My earliest memories are filled with tenderness.
I was born into a home already rich in faith, where the name of God was spoken with love and familiarity.
I learned to love Him before I learned to know Him.
I cannot recall a time when prayer was strange to me; it seemed as natural as breathing.
Even as a child, I felt that I belonged to God, and this sense of belonging gave my soul both joy and seriousness.
I was a child full of affection, perhaps too full.
My heart was ardent, and once it attached itself, it did so entirely.
I loved those around me with a passion that knew no half-measures.
This made me very happy, but it also made me suffer.
A word spoken coldly, a look that seemed indifferent, could wound me deeply.
I did not yet know how to protect my heart; everything reached it directly.
The loss of my dear mother marked me forever.
Though I was very young, the sorrow entered my soul like a shadow that would never completely leave.
From that moment, I became more timid, more sensitive, more inward.
I clung to those I loved with a kind of trembling, fearing always that they too might be taken from me.
I sought reassurance constantly, and when I did not find it, I suffered in silence.
Yet even then, the Good God was watching over me.
He allowed this suffering not to harden my heart, but to deepen it.
He was teaching me, though I did not understand it, that earthly joys are fragile, and that only He remains.
Still, as a child, I felt these things without knowing their meaning.
I only knew that I loved greatly, and that loving greatly often meant suffering greatly.
Very early, I felt drawn toward holiness.
This desire was not vague or distant; it was precise and urgent.
I wanted to be a saint.
Not one day, but now.
Not half-heartedly, but completely.
I wished to give everything to God, to keep nothing for myself.
Yet when I read the lives of the saints, my courage faltered.
They seemed so strong, so heroic, so capable of great sacrifices.
They fasted, they endured torments, they performed wonders.
Compared to them, I felt myself very small.
This troubled me deeply.
I asked myself how a soul like mine
So weak, so easily wounded, so full of imperfections
Could ever reach the heights of sanctity.
I wished to love God as they had loved Him, but I saw clearly that I could not follow the same path.
I feared that my desire for holiness might be an illusion, something beautiful but impossible.
I often pondered why God had created souls so different from one another.
Why did He give such strength to some, and such weakness to others?
Why did He lavish extraordinary graces on certain souls, while others seemed condemned to mediocrity?
These thoughts did not lead me to rebellion, but to a kind of sorrowful confusion.
I loved God too much to believe Him unjust, yet I could not reconcile His goodness with the inequality I perceived.
It was then that He gently answered me, not with a sudden revelation, but with a quiet understanding that entered my soul like light at dawn.
He showed me that His love is not measured by appearances.
He allowed me to see His creation as a whole: the rose, magnificent and admired; the violet ...
Hidden and unnoticed; the daisy, small and simple.
Each has its place.
Each is loved.
The beauty of the garden depends not on uniformity, but on diversity.
I understood then that God does not desire all souls to follow the same path.
He does not call everyone to great deeds or heroic suffering.
Some He calls to remain little, close to the ground, content to be seen only by Him.
Their vocation is not to rise high, but to trust deeply.
This thought brought immense peace to my soul.
For the first time, I saw that my littleness was not a defect, but a calling.
If I could not climb to God by my own efforts, then He Himself would have to descend to me.
This idea filled me with joy.
I resolved to remain small, to accept my weakness, and to rely entirely on His mercy.
I did not yet know how this would unfold, but I felt certain that He would guide me step by step.
As I grew older, the desire to give myself wholly to God became stronger and more precise.
I felt drawn toward a life hidden from the world, a life of prayer and sacrifice.
The Carmel attracted me irresistibly.
Its silence, its separation, its complete offering spoke to my soul more clearly than any other calling.
I wished to belong to God alone, without division, without reserve.
Yet this desire was not without suffering.
I was young, and many doubted my strength and my maturity.
Their hesitation caused me great pain, not because I was proud, but because I feared that my longing might never be fulfilled.
I prayed with fervor, sometimes with confidence, sometimes through tears.
I asked the Blessed Virgin to take my hand and lead me, as a mother leads a timid child.
During this time, I learned that loving God does not spare one from suffering.
On the contrary, it often increases it.
But I also learned that suffering borne with trust becomes light.
Even when my heart was troubled, I felt beneath everything a deep certainty: if God wanted me for Himself ...
Nothing could prevent it.
His will would prevail, not through force, but through love.
Looking back now, I see that these years were the true beginning of my path.
The Good God was teaching me the first lessons of the little way: to accept my weakness, to trust in His mercy, and to abandon myself entirely into His hands.
I did not yet know where this path would lead, but already my soul had learned to walk
Not by strength, but by love.
When at last the Good God opened for me the door I had so long desired, my soul was filled with gratitude and trembling.
I believed that by entering Carmel I was stepping into a place where love would be easy ...
Where my heart would finally rest.
I had given myself without reserve, and I expected ...
Without quite realizing it, that God would take from me my weaknesses in exchange.
He did not.
Instead, He welcomed me exactly as I was, small, fragile, and poor
And asked me to remain so.
The life of Carmel is hidden from the eyes of the world.
It offers no distractions, no great events, no outward signs of success.
At first, this simplicity delighted me.
I felt as though I had found my place at last, a corner where my soul could disappear entirely into God.
Yet very soon I discovered that solitude does not hide one from oneself.
On the contrary, it reveals everything.
In the silence of the cloister, my imperfections rose up before me with a clarity that astonished me.
I had hoped that by withdrawing from the world I would escape the small irritations of daily life, but they followed me inside the enclosure.
A word spoken too sharply, a manner that seemed cold, a gesture that wounded my sensitive heart
These little trials affected me far more than I wished to admit.
I saw clearly that I was still very imperfect, still governed by feelings, still wounded by trifles.
This realization humbled me deeply.
I had dreamed of becoming a saint through generous sacrifices and heroic acts, yet here I was struggling to bear the smallest contradictions.
I was tempted at times to discouragement.
I asked myself how a soul so weak could ever love God as He deserved.
I felt my nothingness pressing upon me, and there were moments when I feared that my vocation itself might be an illusion.
Yet the Good God was watching over me, even in this confusion.
He allowed me to see my misery, not to discourage me, but to detach me from myself.
Little by little, I began to understand that holiness does not consist in being without faults, but in loving God in spite of them.
I saw that my weakness, accepted with humility ...
Could become a source of strength, not because it was pleasing in itself, but because it drew me closer to Divine Mercy.
I soon recognized that I would never be able to imitate the great saints in their extraordinary penances.
My health was delicate, my strength limited, and my nature too sensitive to endure severe austerities.
At first, this realization saddened me.
I wished to suffer greatly for love of God; I longed to prove my devotion through visible sacrifices.
But the more I tried to force myself into a path that was not mine, the more I felt my helplessness.
It was then that the Good God taught me a gentler, yet more demanding way.
He showed me that love is not measured by the greatness of our actions, but by the love with which they are done.
He placed before me a path that was within my reach: to do little things with great love ...
To transform the smallest acts of daily life into offerings pleasing to Him.
I resolved to seek out these little sacrifices, not because they were easy, but because they were hidden.
If I felt repugnance toward a sister, I would try to respond with kindness.
If I was tempted to speak sharply, I would remain silent.
If my duties were monotonous or tiring, I would perform them as though they were precious ...
Knowing that God sees what is hidden.
These acts cost me more than great penances would have, for they required constant vigilance and self-forgetfulness.
Often, no one noticed these efforts.
Sometimes they were even misunderstood.
But this mattered little to me, for I felt that God alone was the witness of my love.
I discovered a strange joy in being unknown, in working without being seen, in loving without being thanked.
It seemed to me that this hidden life was more in harmony with the Gospel than any outward success.
Still, I failed often.
My heart would grow weary, my patience would falter, and I would fall back into my old sensitivities.
Each failure brought me a new lesson.
Instead of dwelling on my misery, I learned to cast myself immediately into God's arms.
I understood that a child who falls does not cease to be loved; she only needs to rise and continue walking ...
Trusting in the one who guides her.
This trust became the foundation of my spiritual life.
I ceased to measure my progress by feelings or by visible achievements.
Consolations in prayer became rare, and dryness frequent.
Yet I learned that love does not consist in feeling, but in choosing.
When prayer was sweet, I thanked God.
When it was barren, I offered Him my fidelity.
In both cases, I sought to love Him equally.
It was during these years that the way of spiritual childhood became fully clear to me.
I saw that my soul was not called to climb the steep staircase of perfection by its own efforts.
That staircase seemed far too high for my short steps.
Instead, I asked God to take me in His arms and lift me to Himself.
I placed all my confidence in His mercy, believing that He would accomplish in me what I could not do alone.
This abandonment brought peace to my soul.
I no longer feared my weaknesses; I embraced them as the very means by which I approached God.
I no longer sought to be admired or understood; I desired only to love.
The smallest act, performed with this intention, seemed to take on an infinite value.
My life, though outwardly insignificant, was filled with meaning.
There were moments, however, when this path was tested.
I experienced misunderstandings, interior trials, and periods of deep dryness.
At times, I felt as though my efforts were useless, my love unnoticed.
But even then, I clung to my resolution to remain little.
I reminded myself that love proves itself most fully when it is stripped of all consolation.
Little by little, my heart was purified.
I ceased to desire anything for myself.
My joy became to please God, even when it cost me everything.
I understood that true freedom lies not in doing what one wishes, but in loving without reserve.
Looking back on these years, I see that the Good God was shaping my soul through the ordinary events of daily life.
He was teaching me that holiness is accessible to all, not because it is easy, but because it rests entirely on love.
The little way, so simple in appearance, demands the gift of one's whole heart.
And it was along this hidden path that He was leading me, step by step, toward Himself.
As the years passed, I felt that the Good God was drawing me closer to Himself ...
Not by filling my soul with light, but by emptying it more and more of everything that was not Him.
I had asked to be little, and He took me at my word.
He allowed me to experience my weakness in ways I had never imagined, and He asked of me, at the end ...
Not great works, but a love that would remain when everything else was taken away.
When the first signs of my illness appeared, I received them with peace.
I had long desired to suffer for love of Jesus, and I thought that perhaps now He was granting me the privilege of being more closely united to His Passion.
At first the suffering was bearable, and even sweet, because I could offer it joyfully.
My strength diminished, my body grew more frail, and I began to feel the weight of fatigue in the smallest actions.
But I still believed that the greatest trial would be physical pain.
I did not know that God was preparing for me a martyrdom of another kind.
As my illness progressed, the sufferings of the body became intense.
There were moments when it seemed impossible to endure.
The fever, the weakness, the oppression of the chest, the helplessness of a body that could no longer obey the will
These things humbled me profoundly.
I who had wished to do so much for God was reduced to doing almost nothing.
Even turning in bed required assistance.
At times my breath was so difficult that each moment felt like a struggle.
Yet in these sufferings, there was also a strange grace: I was forced to remain little.
There was no longer any possibility of relying on myself, no longer any illusion of strength.
I tried, as much as I could, not to be a burden.
My greatest fear was not death, nor pain, but causing trouble to those around me.
I did not want my sisters to be weary because of me.
I wished to give joy even while suffering, to remain gentle even when everything in me cried out.
I understood then more than ever that charity is not a feeling, but a continual gift of self.
But the Good God asked of me something still more painful.
In the midst of my bodily suffering, a darkness descended upon my soul
A darkness so thick that it seemed to blot out Heaven itself.
Until then, the thought of eternal life had been my consolation.
I had longed for Heaven with the simple confidence of a child, believing it to be my true home ...
The place where love would finally be complete.
Suddenly, that certainty was shaken, not by reasoning, but by a trial that touched the very roots of faith.
It seemed to me at times as though the thought of Heaven was only an illusion ...
A beautiful dream invented to soothe the heart.
Words that once filled me with joy now seemed empty.
The promise of eternal life appeared distant and unreal.
It was as though I was hearing within me the voices of those who do not believe, who mock hope ...
Who see death as a final end.
These voices did not come from outside, but from within the depths of my own mind, and they wounded me terribly.
This trial was not a temptation that passed quickly.
It remained, day after day, like a heavy cloud.
I could no longer pray with the sweet certainty I had known.
When I tried to lift my heart to God, I found only dryness.
When I spoke of Heaven, I felt as though I was speaking into a void.
The very thing that had been my joy
Confidence
Seemed to be taken from me.
And yet, in this darkness, I did not cease to love.
I understood that faith is not always light.
Sometimes it is simply fidelity.
Sometimes it is the act of holding onto God when everything within us says that He is far away.
I resolved then to make acts of faith not because I felt them, but because I chose them.
I would believe, not because Heaven seemed near, but because Jesus is Truth.
I would hope, not because my heart was consoled, but because God cannot deceive.
This trial, though painful beyond words, gave my love a purity I had never known.
I was no longer loving God for His gifts, for the sweetness of prayer, for the joy of thinking of Heaven.
I was loving Him in naked faith, in darkness, with no reward.
I felt that this was my true offering, my true martyrdom
Not the blood of the body, but the anguish of the soul.
Often I thought of souls who live without faith, who cannot see beyond the present life ...
Who fear death because it seems to them an absolute end.
I understood that my darkness made me nearer to them.
I offered my trial for them, begging God to let my suffering be of use ...
That those who are far from Him might receive light.
If my soul had to pass through night, perhaps others would find dawn.
Even when I could not pray with words, I prayed with love.
There were moments when I could say nothing to Jesus, but I would turn toward Him like a child in distress who cannot speak, yet who knows that her Father understands.
And when those around me asked what I was doing, I could answer simply: I am loving.
That was all I could do, and it seemed to me that it was everything.
As the end approached, my body grew weaker and my sufferings increased.
There were hours when the pain was so great that I could not rest, when each breath felt like an effort ...
When the nights seemed endless.
And yet, even then, I did not regret having offered myself to Divine Love.
I did not regret the little way.
I understood that love is proved precisely when it is most costly.
There were moments of fear, for nature trembles before death.
I did not always feel brave.
Sometimes I felt only weakness, only helplessness.
But even in these moments, I placed myself in the arms of God.
I did not rely on my own strength, which I did not possess.
I relied on His mercy.
I knew that if I was saved, it would be by love alone.
I had never desired to present myself before God with merits.
I wished to come before Him empty-handed, like a child who has nothing, and who expects everything from her Father.
This confidence did not disappear in my last days.
On the contrary, it became more simple.
I felt that the Good God was not asking me to be strong, but to abandon myself completely.
As I suffered, I felt also a growing certainty that my mission would not end with my death.
I had spoken often, perhaps too boldly, of my desire to spend my Heaven doing good upon earth.
This desire did not come from pride, but from love.
I wanted to continue loving, and love does not know how to be inactive.
I believed that the Good God, who had placed in my heart the desire to help souls ...
Would not extinguish it at the moment when I would be united to Him.
I did not imagine doing extraordinary things.
I did not dream of visible miracles or of grand works.
I wanted to be like a little flower scattering its petals, like a shower of roses
Little acts of love, little graces, little helps given to souls who are struggling.
I wanted to make known the little way, to tell souls that holiness is not beyond them ...
That Jesus does not call only the strong, but delights to lift up the weak.
In my last days, when speech became difficult and strength almost gone ...
My soul remained fixed on one truth: God is Love.
Even when I could not feel His presence, even when faith was dark, I clung to this truth.
I had chosen Him, and I knew that He had chosen me first.
That is the secret of everything.
When at last the final moment came, it was not as I had imagined in childhood.
It was not triumphant, not filled with sweetness, but it was peaceful in its surrender.
I did not claim Heaven as a right.
I received it as mercy.
My soul passed from this world as it had lived within it: little, poor, and trusting.
If the Good God has permitted my life to be told, it is not to show great deeds, for I have done none.
It is to show His mercy, which is able to make a path for the smallest souls.
I would like to repeat to every soul what I have learned: do not be afraid of your weakness.
Do not be discouraged by your falls.
Only one thing wounds Jesus, only one thing grieves His Heart, and that is want of confidence.
Trust Him.
Love Him.
Be little.
And if He grants me the grace to do good on earth after my death, it will be only to lead souls to this same confidence.
I have not sought any other glory than to be loved by God, and to love Him in return.
That is my whole story, my whole desire, my whole Heaven.
